newsitem.title: UK: CBI looks to era of cooperation with UK government.
newsitem.headline: CBI looks to era of cooperation with UK government.

text.p: Britain's top employers group the Confederation of British Industry on Tuesday looked to an era of cooperation with the new Labour government and said even policies it disagreed with may not damage the economy.

CBI president Colin Marshall told the industry group's annual meeting there were many areas of Labour policy it supported although it remained concerned about a minimum wage, the European Union Social Chapter and a windfall tax on Britain's privatised utilities.

"Not everything in the New Labour garden appears rosy to us," he said. "But there is the distinct prospect of working with ministers and their officials to ensure that policies we presently view with caution, emerge as legislation which does not harm Britain's commercial and industrial competitiveness."
He pleaded for the government to maintain an economic backdrop of sensible and stable growth and said he hoped the CBI could persuade it to take the rough edges off policies that could hit industry.
The government has pledged to introduce a national minimum wage after consultation with worker and employer leaders.

The CBI has said a floor for wages will not unduly hurt British industry, or cost jobs, if it was set at less than 3.50 pounds an hour. But earlier this week the public sector union Unison, Britain's largest, demanded a minimum of 4.42 pounds.

On the European Union Social Chapter, which Labour will sign up to, business leaders have said it is not so much the two directives the protocol currently boasts -- on parental leave and consultation rights for employees of multinational companies -- that concern them, it is more what might be introduced in the future.

Marshall said, even though the CBI was worried about the Social Chapter, the new Labour government had eased many of its concerns. "We have come to be reassured by the government's pledge on maintaining Britain's flexible markets and to spreading our best practice across Europe."
But he told Labour, Britain's veto on further EU workplace legislation must be maintained.

As for the windfall tax on the privatised utilities, Marshall said the CBI continued to oppose it although the government's plans to use the money raised to help 250,000 people into work are welcomed by many industry leaders.

"I do not, for one minute, believe that there is any chance of persuading the government to turn away from these plans, and neither would there be any percentage in attempting to do so," Marshall said.
But on a more consensual note, he said the new Labour government and the CBI were as one on education, training and domestic investment.
"Quite simply, people form our most vital, basic raw material. The more educated and skilled they are, the more competitive our goods and services become."

Marshall also backed Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's assertion that investment in Britain is far too low, but gave a guarded warning against introducing measures that penalise profitable companies.

"The level of business investment does need to be stepped up but that depends on having economic and fiscal policies which allow commerce and industry not just to build profits, but also to retain them," he said.

But he did not allow his reservations to cloud an upbeat message. "These are early days, but the hallmark of our relationship so far with the new government is promise -- the promise of cooperation and partnership."
